title: Count Good Triplets
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every triple directly versus fixing two indices and using a Fenwick tree over values to count the third in bulk.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of integers arr, and integers a, b, c, count the number of "good" index triples (i, j, k), with i less than j less than k, satisfying all three conditions: the absolute difference between arr[i] and arr[j] is at most a, between arr[j] and arr[k] is at most b, and between arr[i] and arr[k] is at most c.

blocks.text: Count every index triple i less than j less than k where arr[i] and arr[j] are close (within a), arr[j] and arr[k] are close (within b), and arr[i] and arr[k] are close (within c).

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Chains of Three Closely-Matched Runners
blocks.text: Picture runners with certain speeds, and needing to count every ordered trio where consecutive pairs (and the two endpoints) all have sufficiently similar speeds, within specific tolerances for each pairing.

blocks.caption: Fix the first pair, then count valid third indices with a value in a range, using a Fenwick tree

blocks.text: There are 4 valid triples satisfying all three conditions.

Before checking every triple directly, notice that fixing the first two indices reduces the third condition to counting values within a range, at positions after the second index, exactly what a Fenwick tree over values can answer quickly.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For a fixed pair i, j satisfying the first condition, the valid values of k are exactly those positions greater than j whose value falls within BOTH [arr[j] minus b, arr[j] plus b] AND [arr[i] minus c, arr[i] plus c], a single combined range.

Observation 2: Counting how many values within a range exist among positions greater than j is a range-count query, answerable in O(log maxValue) with a Fenwick tree indexed by value.

Observation 3: Processing j from 0 to n minus 1, and maintaining a Fenwick tree that always represents exactly "positions greater than the current j," lets each pair (i, j) query that tree directly.

Observation 4: Removing arr[j] from the Fenwick tree exactly once, right before processing pairs with that j, keeps the tree correctly restricted to positions greater than j at every step.

This leads to maintaining a Fenwick tree over values, initially containing every element, removing arr[j] as j advances (so the tree always represents positions greater than j), and for every valid (i, j) pair, range-querying the combined value range for valid k.
Check every index triple i less than j less than k directly against all three conditions.

items: Loop i from 0 to n minus 1, j from i plus 1 to n minus 1, k from j plus 1 to n minus 1.
Check all three pairwise closeness conditions.
Count every triple that satisfies all three.

codes.python:
def count_good_triplets(arr, a, b, c):
    n = len(arr)
    count = 0
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            for k in range(j + 1, n):                # every triple, checked directly
                if (abs(arr[i] - arr[j]) <= a and
                        abs(arr[j] - arr[k]) <= b and
                        abs(arr[i] - arr[k]) <= c):
                    count += 1
    return count

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every one of the roughly n cubed over 6 triples is generated and checked directly against all three conditions.
No structure is reused between different triples, even when they share the same i, j pair.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed), every triple examined directly.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: for a fixed i, j pair, every valid k just needs to satisfy a value-range condition, but the brute force still checks every individual k directly instead of counting matching values in bulk.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every k individually is wasteful: for a fixed i, j pair, the valid k values are exactly those (at positions greater than j) whose value falls within a specific combined range, a count that can be answered directly instead of checked one at a time.

What structure answers "how many values in a range, among positions greater than j" quickly: a Fenwick tree indexed by value, from which elements are removed as j advances, so it always represents exactly the positions still ahead.

The core idea: process j left to right, remove arr[j] from the Fenwick tree right before considering pairs ending at j, then for each valid i less than j, range-query the combined value bounds to count matching k values in O(log maxValue).

Build a Fenwick tree over the value range, initially containing every element of arr. Process j from 0 to n minus 1: first remove arr[j] from the tree (so it now represents only positions greater than j). Then for every i less than j with arr[i] and arr[j] close enough (within a), compute the combined valid range for arr[k], [max(arr[j] minus b, arr[i] minus c), min(arr[j] plus b, arr[i] plus c)], and add the Fenwick tree's range count for that range to the answer.

Removing arr[j] from the Fenwick tree exactly when j is reached guarantees the tree always represents exactly the elements at positions strictly greater than j, matching the required k less than... wait, k greater than j. For a valid (i, j) pair, the combined range [max(arr[j] minus b, arr[i] minus c), min(arr[j] plus b, arr[i] plus c)] captures exactly the values that satisfy both the j-to-k and i-to-k closeness conditions simultaneously; a single range-count query on the position-restricted Fenwick tree counts every valid k for that pair directly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared log maxValue), for every valid (i, j) pair, one O(log maxValue) range query.
Space: O(maxValue) for the Fenwick tree.

blocks.text: Count Good Triplets shows how fixing two of three loop variables, and turning the third into a value-range COUNT rather than an individual check, lets a Fenwick tree cut an O(n cubed) search down to O(n squared log maxValue).

items: Removing arr[j] from the Fenwick tree at the wrong time, breaking the "represents positions greater than j" invariant.
Forgetting to intersect BOTH range constraints (from the j-k condition and the i-k condition) into a single combined range before querying.

blocks.text: Presenting the O(n cubed) brute force first (often sufficient given small constraints), then explaining how fixing i, j and counting valid k with a Fenwick tree improves it, shows both practical awareness and a stronger technique in reserve.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you do better than n cubed", think: fix two indices, and use a Fenwick tree over values to count the third index's valid range directly.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n cubed) time; the optimized Fenwick tree approach runs in O(n squared log maxValue) time. Space is O(1) for the brute force and O(maxValue) for the optimized approach.

items: Pattern: fix two loop variables, count the third with a Fenwick tree over values restricted by position.
Core Idea: process j left to right, removing arr[j] from a value-indexed Fenwick tree so it always represents positions greater than j; for each valid (i,j) pair, range-count valid k values directly.
Time: O(n cubed) for the brute force, O(n squared log maxValue) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(maxValue) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: for a fixed pair, valid third indices form a value range, countable directly instead of checked one at a time.
Interview Difficulty: the brute force is often accepted given small constraints; the Fenwick tree optimization demonstrates a stronger technique.
One line memory trick: fix i, j; Fenwick-tree-count valid k values in a combined range, restricted to positions after j.
